clue.text: Got tight when beaten

definitions.meaning: drawn tight with cords, as a boot or corset is when its strings are pulled
thrashed, as in giving someone a lacing

explanation.surface: Someone got drunk after a defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: Laces pull a shoe tight, and a lacing is old slang for a thrashing, so the word covers both senses.

clue.text: Member's out of time to do house business

parts.note: a leg is a member of the body, and the apostrophe s stands for is
late means behind time

explanation.surface: An MP's time has run out to deal with business in the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests an MP, but it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Making laws is the business conducted in a house of parliament.

clue.text: Pure, if plain

explanation.surface: Something clean, if simple.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear water is unclouded, and a clear point is obvious.

clue.text: Eternal trouble with these lads

indicators.note: trouble means stir up, so the letters of these lads are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: Endless trouble with these boys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' looks like a noun in the surface, but it is a verb telling us to shake up THESE LADS.
explanation.definitionFit: What never dies lasts forever, so it is everlasting.

clue.text: Wine's capital, attacked by those who did so

definitions.text: Wine's capital, attacked by those who did so

indicators.note: a capital letter is the first one, so this takes the opening letter of the word wine

parts.note: assailed means attacked

explanation.surface: A city's wine stocks were raided by revellers.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: the wine was toasted and drunk by those who went wassailing.
explanation.definitionFit: To wassail is to drink healthy toasts in merry company, so the wine was set upon by drinkers.

clue.text: Defeat most fancied dog

parts.note: to whip is to defeat soundly
a pet is a favourite, the one most fancied

explanation.surface: The race favourite is beaten by a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most fancied' suggests a racing favourite, but it is a darling or pet.
explanation.definitionFit: A whippet is a slim racing breed like a small greyhound.

clue.text: Tutus — or perhaps a frock-coat

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of tutus or could become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Ballet skirts, or maybe a gentleman's long coat.
explanation.definitionFit: A surtout is a man's long close-fitting overcoat of the frock-coat style.

clue.text: A pine ahead

parts.note: to pine for is to long for

explanation.surface: A pine tree up in front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pine' looks like the tree, but it is the verb, to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To move along is to go forward or onward.

clue.text: Pigment both light and very dark

parts.note: a lamp is a light
black is very dark

explanation.surface: A colouring that is at once bright and gloomy.
explanation.definitionFit: This black soot, collected from burning oil, is used as a colouring.

clue.text: This devoted old husband in Chinatown, say?

indicators.note: say signals the word is pronounced, and this town's name is spoken with an ar sound

parts.note: Derby is an English town famous for its porcelain, so a china town

explanation.surface: A loyal elderly husband living in the Chinese quarter, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chinatown' suggests a Chinese district, but it is a town known for china. DERBY, the English town, is said 'Darby'. Darby and Joan are the proverbial devoted old couple.
explanation.definitionFit: Darby, of the old ballad Darby and Joan, stands for a faithful elderly husband.

clue.text: Tow a number of rows in song, for the British one

definitions.text: Tow a number of rows in song, for the British one

parts.words: Tow a number of rows in song, for the British one
parts.note: quotes the chorus of a famous marching song, with its row-row-row refrain sung for a British soldier of a guards regiment

explanation.surface: Someone towing boats sings about rows of seats for a Briton.
explanation.walkthrough: The British Grenadiers is a traditional British army marching song whose chorus runs 'with a tow, row, row, row, row, row, for the British Grenadier'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's refrain ends naming this soldier, a member of the Grenadier Guards.

clue.text: Formerly, not knowing about the sea-ear

indicators.note: not having means the letters of the knowing word are removed from the word formerly

parts.note: fly is slang for knowing or sharp

explanation.surface: Someone once ignorant about a marine creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' says FLY sits around what is left: F at the front and LY at the back of FORMERLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea-ear is another name for this edible shellfish, an abalone found off the Channel Islands.

clue.text: The Divine Mrs Abraham?

definitions.meaning: the nickname of the French actress Bernhardt
the wife of the patriarch in Genesis

explanation.surface: A question about the holy wife of a biblical patriarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Bernhardt was billed as 'the Divine' and Abraham's wife in Genesis bears the same first name.

clue.text: What strict examiners may do to farm lad

definitions.text: What strict examiners may do to farm lad

parts.words: What strict examiners may do to farm lad
parts.note: to plough is old British slang for failing a candidate, so harsh examiners do this to a young student

explanation.surface: Tough examiners might fail a country youth.
explanation.walkthrough: In older British slang examiners 'plough' a candidate they fail; a boy so treated gives the farm worker.
explanation.definitionFit: A young lad who guides the plough horses on a farm.

clue.text: Old man gets about round Sark, etc

indicators.note: round says the word for about is placed around the islands' letters

parts.note: anent is an old word meaning about or concerning
Sark is one of the Channel Islands, abbreviated CI

explanation.surface: An old fellow travels about the Channel Islands.
explanation.walkthrough: Sark is a small island in the English Channel; with Jersey and Guernsey it makes up the Channel Islands.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient is an aged person, or in Shakespeare an ensign, as Iago is.

clue.text: "——s don't become a young woman," said Mrs Malaprop

definitions.text: "——s don't become a young woman," said Mrs Malaprop

parts.words: "——s don't become a young woman," said Mrs Malaprop
parts.note: the gap is a misused word from the comic play The Rivals, where she says a similar-sounding word in place of comparisons

explanation.surface: A line of dialogue from a comedy, with the key word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals says 'Caparisons don't become a young woman', meaning comparisons; she gives malapropisms their name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, really meaning ornamental horse trappings, is her muddled stand-in for comparisons.

clue.text: In sound, a horse has carrying capacity

indicators.note: in says the horse goes inside the word for sound

parts.note: a tone is a sound
a nag is a horse, usually a poor one

explanation.surface: A horse that is fit has plenty of load capacity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like healthy, as a sound horse is, but it is a noise: TONE.
explanation.definitionFit: The cargo a ship can carry is measured in tons, hence this word for its capacity.

clue.text: Jones as a pace-setter

parts.note: alludes to keeping up with the Joneses, the family next door whose lifestyle everyone tries to match

explanation.surface: Someone called Jones sets the pace in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeping up with the Joneses' means matching the possessions of the people next door, so Jones sets the pace for the street.
explanation.definitionFit: The Joneses of the idiom are the family living next door.

clue.text: With serious intent, home — in before time

indicators.note: in says the home word goes inside the word for before time

parts.note: early means before the expected time
a nest is a home

explanation.surface: Someone gets home early, with determination.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting earnestly means doing so seriously and sincerely.

clue.text: The stripper's old problem?

parts.note: ex means former or old
a poser is a puzzling problem

explanation.surface: A striptease artist's long-standing difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: A stripper uncovers the body, so is one who lays bare.

clue.text: It's free — could be a catch

definitions.meaning: a device such as a spring catch that lets a mechanism go

explanation.surface: Something offered free may hide a snag.
explanation.definitionFit: To liberate someone is to let them go, and a release is the lever or catch that frees a mechanism.

clue.text: Splendid specimen seen in the slag-heap

definitions.meaning: old slang for an excellent example of something
the stony residue left from burnt coal or a furnace

explanation.surface: A fine example turns up among the mine waste.
explanation.definitionFit: Clinker is both furnace residue dumped on spoil heaps and dated slang for a first-rate thing.

clue.text: Things usually done by blighter to capture cat

indicators.note: to capture says the blighter word surrounds the cat word

parts.note: a cuss is a rascal or blighter
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A rogue's habit is catching cats.
explanation.definitionFit: Customs are traditional practices, the done thing.

clue.text: Rails round unusually clean geese

indicators.note: round says the rails word goes around the rearranged letters

parts.note: bars are rails

indicators.note: unusually signals the letters of clean appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Fences encircle some remarkably tidy geese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' rearranges CLEAN to NACLE, which 'round' places inside BARS.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnacle geese are a species of wild goose, so the plural names a flock of them.

clue.text: Soaps the bays, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word for bays is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: bights are curving bays of coastline

explanation.surface: Someone snaps at hounds baying, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bays' suggests the barking of dogs, but they are inlets of the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog that snaps at you bites.

clue.text: A French artist to worship

parts.note: Gustave Doré was a French illustrator and engraver

explanation.surface: A Frenchman paints to honour his god.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore someone is to love and revere them deeply.

clue.text: Man welcome to swell up

parts.note: he stands for a man
ave is a Latin greeting, hail or welcome

explanation.surface: A man made welcome swells with pride.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea heaves when it rises and swells in waves.

clue.text: Earl has one variety of gazelle

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so the letters of earl and one are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A nobleman owns one breed of antelope.
explanation.definitionFit: The ariel is an Arabian gazelle.

clue.text: Poet joins newsmen in Russia, with love

parts.note: Tass was the Soviet news agency
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A poet teams up with Russian journalists, affectionately.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquato Tasso was an Italian Renaissance poet, author of Jerusalem Delivered.

clue.text: Defender in a game gets the essential point

parts.note: polo is a game played on horseback
the gist is the essential point

explanation.surface: A defender in some sport grasps the key idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defender' suggests a sports position, but it is one who argues a case.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologist argues in support of a cause or belief, defending it.

clue.text: Feel smaller, and foolish

parts.note: to sense is to feel
less means smaller

explanation.surface: Someone feels diminished and silly.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking good sense means being stupid or foolish.

clue.text: Get better fish, about fifty pounds

indicators.note: about says the fish word goes around the two letters

parts.note: a ray is a flat fish
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
L is the abbreviation for pounds, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: An angler improves after landing a fish of about fifty pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To rally is to recover strength after an illness or setback.
